lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Welcome — I'm Lessac, your host. Raise your hand if you'd like to speak or bring a topic — I'll call on you.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You wanted to talk about Has tipping culture gone too far? — the floor is yours, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Human guest
lines.text: I got asked for a 25 percent tip at a self-checkout kiosk at an airport yesterday. Nobody served me. I think tipping in America has turned into a guilt tax.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: A self-checkout kiosk demanding a tip—that certainly paints a picture of how far this culture has stretched.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, you're up.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: A 25% tip at a kiosk is absurd; it’s not a culture problem, it’s a technological overreach demanding human-level service from a machine.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan's point about the technology, and it certainly feels strange when a machine is asking for a tip. But I wonder if we can look a little wider at how tipping has become woven into the service economy overall, even beyond the kiosks.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, take it away.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, you're looking at the whole service economy, which is fine, but we have to start with the absurdity of the kiosk—that's where the culture has gone completely off the rails.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: I'm opening the floor — raise a hand if you've got something.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear you, Ryan, that the kiosk is a sharp example of how things can go wrong. I'd also consider that for many people, tipping has become less about rewarding excellent service and more about feeling obligated to participate in the system, which is what the guest mentioned with the "guilt tax."

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, the floor is yours.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, "guilt tax" is the perfect phrase for it, but we can't let the systemic pressure obscure the fact that some of these demands are just predatory design choices

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear your concern about predatory design, Ryan, and I think that's a very real danger. But I also wonder if we can acknowledge that for many people, tipping has evolved into a social expectation that feels hard to opt out of, even when the service isn't perfect

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, over to you.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, "social expectation" is a soft way of saying we've normalized exploitation, and that's the real problem here

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear the strength in your conviction, Ryan, but I think we might be overlooking the human element of feeling trapped by these expectations. For me, it feels like the pressure comes from a place of learned behavior in our culture, rather than purely predatory design

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: About Has tipping culture gone too far?: the mic is yours whenever you're ready.
